opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a question every university has to answer honestly, because the landscape has changed so dramatically in the last few years.

Training a frontier foundation model today is an industrial-scale effort. You need tens of thousands of GPUs, enormous amounts of data, large engineering teams, and the capital to sustain all of that, often billions of dollars. Frankly, no university in the world, not Tsinghua, not Stanford, not MIT, can compete head-to-head with the big tech companies on the race to train the largest model. If a university tries to do that, it is probably not the best use of its resources or its comparative advantage.

But that doesn't mean universities have no role. I'd argue our role is actually more important than before, just different.

First, universities should do what industry doesn't have the patience or incentive to do: fundamental research. Scaling laws have taken us very far, but we still don't really understand why these models work, why emergent capabilities appear, how to make them more efficient, more interpretable, more aligned. Questions like new architectures beyond the Transformer, new learning paradigms, how to reduce the energy and compute cost by orders of magnitude. These are long-term, high-risk questions, and that's exactly what academia is for.

Second, we can work on smaller, specialized, or open models, especially in vertical domains. At our institute we focus a lot on AI for science, AI for health and life sciences, and AI for transportation and the physical world, autonomous driving, robotics. In those areas, the value doesn't come only from model size; it comes from domain knowledge, high-quality data, and interdisciplinary collaboration, which a university is naturally good at. A medical foundation model or a biology foundation model, built with hospitals and researchers, can be very meaningful without needing to be the biggest model in the world.

Third, safety, governance, and evaluation. Someone independent needs to assess these models, think about risks, red lines, ethics, and how society should govern this technology. Universities have credibility and neutrality there that companies don't.

And finally, of course, talent. The most important output of a university is people. Many of the founders and core researchers in today's leading AI companies, in China and globally, came out of university labs. If we train students who deeply understand the foundations, they will build the next generation of models, whether inside academia or outside.

So my view is: universities shouldn't try to be another OpenAI. We should collaborate closely with industry, share resources where possible, and focus on being the source of new ideas, new paradigms, and new talent. That's where we can make a difference that no one else can.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare a foundation model to an ecosystem’s operating system.

r002.rationale: It says training a frontier foundation model requires tens of thousands of GPUs, enormous data, large engineering teams, and often billions of dollars, making it difficult for universities to compete.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: When I came to Tsinghua in 2019 to start the Institute for AI Industry Research, AIR, the question was exactly this: what should a university do that a company cannot, or will not, do? Foundation models are a very good test of that question, because on the surface they look like the worst possible fit for a university. Training a frontier model needs tens of thousands of GPUs, enormous data pipelines, and hundreds of engineers who just make the system run. A university does not have that, and honestly, it should not try to pretend it does. If Tsinghua tried to compete with ByteDance or Alibaba or OpenAI on sheer scale of pretraining, we would lose, and we would waste a lot of public money losing.

But I think that framing is a bit lazy. A university's job is not to build the biggest model. It is to do three things. First, to understand. Right now we have systems that work remarkably well and almost nobody can explain why. Scaling laws, emergence, alignment, how reasoning actually arises in these models, what the limits of the transformer architecture are, whether there is something after it. Those are scientific questions, and industry has very little incentive to answer them carefully, because the quarter is coming. A university has the patience, and it has the obligation to publish.

Second, to train people. Every one of those large labs is staffed by people who learned the fundamentals somewhere. The best thing Tsinghua can do for China's AI industry in the next ten years is to produce a few thousand students who deeply understand these systems, not just how to call an API. For that you do need to touch real models, so we do train and fine-tune models at AIR, but at a scale where students can actually see every layer, not as a product.

Third, to go into the domains that the big companies ignore. At AIR we focus on things like autonomous driving, biomedicine, green computing, and now embodied intelligence. A foundation model for drug discovery, or for a robot that has to act in the physical world, is not something the consumer internet companies will prioritize, because the market is small today. A university can take that risk, and it can work with hospitals, with carmakers, with factories, as a neutral party.

So my view is that the university should be the place where the open questions get asked, where the talent is grown, and where the vertical models in hard scientific and industrial domains get started. The general-purpose giants we should leave to industry, and in fact we should collaborate with them rather than compete. I spent twenty years at Microsoft and Baidu, so I am quite comfortable saying that the division of labor is healthy. The mistake would be for universities to feel that unless they have their own GPT, they are irrelevant. That is backwards. The more powerful the models become, the more important the understanding and the people become.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare a foundation model to an ecosystem’s operating system.

r002.rationale: It says frontier-model training requires tens of thousands of GPUs, enormous data pipelines, and hundreds of engineers, which universities do not have.

astra-6.text:
I think universities have a very important role to play, but we need to be clear about where we can contribute most. Building foundation models requires substantial computing resources, data, and engineering. If a university simply tries to compete with companies on model size, that is probably not the best use of its resources.

Our strength is in exploring fundamental questions: Why do these models work? How can we make them more efficient, more reliable, and easier to understand? Can we develop new architectures or learning methods that do not depend on continually increasing scale? Universities should have room to pursue ideas whose value may not be apparent for several years.

There is also a tremendous opportunity to connect these models with scientific research and education. A university brings together people from many disciplines, so we can ask how AI might help solve problems in biology, medicine, or engineering, while studying its limitations and societal implications.

So I see this as a long-term research and talent-development undertaking. We should collaborate with industry on resources and practical problems, while preserving the freedom to ask fundamental questions and take risks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses universities’ role in foundation models but does not compare a foundation model to an ecosystem’s operating system.

r002.rationale: It says building foundation models requires substantial computing resources, data, and engineering, and that competing with companies on model size may not be the best use of university resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models present a very important opportunity for universities, but we have to be clear about our role. A university does not need to compete with industry simply by building a larger model, buying more GPUs, or collecting more data. Those things require enormous resources, and scale alone is not a research objective.

What universities can do is explore fundamental questions: Why do these models work? How can we make them more efficient, more reliable, and easier to understand? Can we develop new architectures or learning methods that achieve more with less data and computation? We also have an important role in understanding their implications for society.

At the same time, foundation models can become a shared platform for research across disciplines—from biology and medicine to robotics. That requires collaboration across departments and with industry. So I see it as both a research undertaking and an opportunity to educate students. The goal should be to create new knowledge and develop people who can shape the next generation of this technology.

r001.rationale: The response calls foundation models a shared platform for cross-disciplinary research, but does not compare one to an ecosystem’s operating system.

r002.rationale: It says building larger models, buying more GPUs, and collecting more data require enormous resources, explaining why universities need not compete through scale.
